world.setting: Occupied France and Nazi Germany during World War II — from the walled coastal citadel of Saint-Malo under American bombardment to the coal-mining orphanages of Zollverein, the grand halls of the Muséum National in Paris, and the brutal corridors of the Schulpforta military academy
world.register: literary historical fiction — lyrical, interwoven timelines, sensory prose

marie-laure.name: Marie-Laure
marie-laure.role: Blind French girl, protagonist — navigates occupied France through touch and intellect, carries the Sea of Flames diamond unknowingly
marie-laure.look: A slight 16-year-old French girl with cloudy pale eyes from congenital cataracts, wavy dark brown hair pulled back with a ribbon, delicate cheekbones, wearing a faded blue cotton dress with a small leather satchel, fingertips tracing the air in front of her.

werner.name: Werner
werner.role: German orphan and radio prodigy — his genius lifts him from the coal mines into a Nazi military academy, where he builds tracking equipment that hunts the people he once admired
werner.look: An 18-year-old German soldier with striking white-blond hair, pale skin, sharp intelligent blue eyes, lean wiry build, wearing a rumpled grey Wehrmacht field uniform with radio headphones around his neck.

daniel.name: Daniel LeBlanc
daniel.role: Marie-Laure's father, master locksmith at the Muséum National — builds the wooden model city, carries a decoy diamond across France
daniel.look: A stocky 45-year-old French craftsman with calloused steady hands, a kind square face, short dark hair greying at the temples, wearing a brown wool museum worker's coat with tiny brass keys on a ring at his belt.

etienne.name: Etienne
etienne.role: Marie-Laure's great-uncle, WWI veteran paralyzed by agoraphobia — broadcasts coded Resistance transmissions from his attic in Saint-Malo
etienne.look: A frail 65-year-old French man with trembling hands, thinning white hair, hollow frightened eyes behind round spectacles, wearing a faded dressing gown over a wrinkled shirt, standing in a dim attic beside a glowing radio transmitter.

vonrumpel.name: von Rumpel
vonrumpel.role: German sergeant major and gemologist — hunts the Sea of Flames diamond across occupied Europe while dying of a tumor
vonrumpel.look: A gaunt 50-year-old German officer with sunken cheeks from terminal illness, close-cropped greying hair, cold analytical grey eyes, wearing a crisp dark Wehrmacht officer's coat with a jeweler's loupe on a chain around his neck.

frederick.name: Frederick
frederick.role: Werner's bunkmate at Schulpforta — gentle bird-watcher who refuses to pour water on a prisoner, beaten into permanent brain damage
frederick.look: A thin 16-year-old German boy with thick round glasses, soft brown eyes, uncombed light brown hair, slight stooped build, wearing the grey wool uniform of the Schulpforta academy with a small bird-identification notebook in his pocket.

jutta.name: Jutta
jutta.role: Werner's younger sister — moral conscience who challenges his complicity with the Nazi machine
jutta.look: A 14-year-old German girl with the same striking white-blond hair as Werner, sharp questioning eyes, a determined set to her jaw, wearing a simple patched orphanage dress.

madame-manec.name: Madame Manec
madame-manec.role: Etienne's elderly housekeeper in Saint-Malo — organizes neighborhood women into a Resistance cell
madame-manec.look: A stout 70-year-old French woman with silver hair in a tight bun, weathered ruddy face, strong broad hands, wearing a practical dark apron over a grey housedress.

narrator.name: Narrator
narrator.role: The voice of the deep dive — analyzing Doerr's craft and the book's argument about sight, complicity, and the weaponization of knowledge
narrator.look: A modern analyst in a dark blazer over an open-collar shirt, gesturing while explaining the themes of All the Light We Cannot See.

everyman.name: Everyman
everyman.role: The modern viewer — a stand-in for anyone navigating an age of competing signals and chosen blindness
everyman.look: A faceless modern figure in a plain dark hoodie, illuminated by the blue glow of a screen, headphones on, surrounded by invisible radio waves.

saint-malo-attic.look: A cramped dusty attic in a tall narrow house in Saint-Malo, wooden rafters, a glowing radio transmitter with coiled wires, a small round window overlooking the burning walled city below

zollverein-orphanage.look: A bleak dormitory in a coal-mining orphanage — iron bunk beds, bare grey walls streaked with soot, a salvaged radio on a wooden crate crackling with a distant French voice

schulpforta-academy.look: A brutal Nazi military academy courtyard in winter — stone walls, uniformed cadets in rigid formation, ice-crusted cobblestones, a flagpole bearing a swastika

paris-museum.look: The grand gallery of the Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle in Paris — glass specimen cases of minerals and shells, high vaulted ceilings, wooden cabinets of curiosities, soft amber light

saint-malo-street.look: A narrow cobblestone street inside the walled citadel of Saint-Malo — medieval stone buildings, salt air, the sound of surf through the ramparts, rubble from recent bombing

shore.look: The rocky Atlantic coast below the walls of Saint-Malo — grey waves crashing against granite, tide pools filled with snails and anemones, salt mist in the air

objects.why: The radio — the central object of the book; invisible waves that connect and betray, the signal that Werner and Etienne both serve
The Sea of Flames diamond — cursed knowledge, power that destroys the holder's loved ones, locked inside a puzzle box
The miniature wooden model of Paris/Saint-Malo that Daniel builds — Marie-Laure's way of seeing the city through fingertips
Light and perception — the book's thesis that blindness is moral not physical, that the brain constructs the world from attention
The 1944 bombardment of Saint-Malo — incendiary rounds, the burning city, destruction as backdrop to the moral convergence
The war machine — Nazi Germany's systematic weaponization of talent, science, and youth into instruments of destruction
Complicity and moral captivity — Werner's silence during Frederick's beating, the thousand small surrenders that constitute collaboration
The bucket of ice water Frederick refuses to pour — the crystallizing moment of moral choice vs. obedience
Moral orientation — which frequency will you serve, which signal will you follow when the choice comes
Von Rumpel's jeweler's loupe — the collector who measures and catalogs beauty while understanding nothing about it
Jules Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues — Marie-Laure reads it into the radio transmitter; knowledge as resistance
Daniel and Marie-Laure's bond — the father who teaches his blind daughter to see through craft and devotion

spine.claim: A blind girl and a radio-building orphan are shaped by opposite forms of perception — touch vs. signal — in a world about to weaponize both.
Science promises Werner freedom but delivers him into the Nazi machine; knowledge stripped of moral compass becomes a tracking instrument that hunts the innocent.
Frederick's refusal to pour the water — and Werner's silence — proves that complicity is not one dramatic betrayal but a thousand tiny silences that accumulate into moral blindness.
Etienne's attic broadcasts and von Rumpel's diamond hunt reveal that the war's real contest is between those who transmit meaning and those who extract possession.
Werner's tracking antenna leads him to the very broadcast that saved his childhood mind — and he chooses the signal over the uniform, proving that the frequency you serve defines who you become.
